source_text:
In Ruth
ΡΟΥΘ.
12.989 Καὶ ὄνομα τῇ δευτέρᾳ Ῥούθ. Ῥοὺθ τύπον φέρει τῶν ἐθνῶν· ἥτις κατέλιπε τὰ
πάτρια, καὶ ἡνώθη τῇ Ἰσραηλιτικῇ ἕξει. Ζητητέον δὲ πῶς, τοῦ νόμου ἀπαγορεύοντος
μὴ εἰσελθεῖν Μοαβίτην εἰς Ἐκκλησίαν Θεοῦ, ἡ Ῥοὺς Μοαβίτις οὖσα εἰσῆλθε. Καὶ
τοῦτο ζητῶν χρῆσαι τῷ· "∆ικαίω δὲ νόμος οὐ κεῖται, ἀλλὰ ἀδίκοις καὶ
ἀνυποτάκτοις."
thought_title: Ruth as a type of the Gentiles and the legal problem of her entry
orientation: Origen opens his commentary on Ruth by identifying Ruth as a type of the Gentiles and then raises the legal difficulty that the law forbids a Moabite from entering the assembly of God.
pass_a_gloss: And [the] name of the second [was] Ruth. Ruth bears [a] type of the Gentiles; who left the ancestral [things], and was joined to the Israelite way [of life]. And [it] must be sought how, the law forbidding [that] a Moabite not enter into [the] assembly of God, Ruth being a Moabite entered. And seeking this, I use the [saying]: "But for the righteous [the] law is not laid down, but for [the] lawless and disobedient."

choices.why: The glossary requires 'type' for τύπον; φέρει is rendered literally as 'bears' to preserve the metaphor of carrying a typological significance.
The neuter plural substantive refers to ancestral traditions or ways; 'ancestral customs' makes the concrete sense clear.
ἕξις means a settled state or condition; 'way of life' captures the sense of a habitual manner of living that Ruth joined.
The verbal adjective expresses necessity; 'must be sought' preserves the impersonal obligation.
χρῆσαι is a middle imperative of χράομαι meaning 'use/apply'; the dative τῷ points to the quoted saying. 'Use the saying' preserves the imperative force and the hermeneutical application.
κεῖται is the perfect of κεῖμαι meaning 'is established/laid down' for laws; 'is not laid down' preserves the legal metaphor.

bible_refs.note: δικαίῳ δὲ νόμος οὐ κεῖται, ἀλλὰ ἀδίκοις καὶ ἀνυποτάκτοις

pass_b_english: And the name of the second was Ruth. Ruth bears a type of the Gentiles, for she left behind her ancestral customs and was joined to the Israelite way of life. But we must ask how Ruth, being a Moabite, entered the assembly of God when the law forbids a Moabite from entering. And seeking this, I apply the saying: “The law is not laid down for the righteous, but for the lawless and disobedient” (1 Timothy 1:9).

problems.quote: As you seek this out, use the saying
problems.why: English makes Origen address 'you'; Greek has him speaking of himself ('I, seeking this, apply/use').
problems.fix: And seeking this, I apply the saying
problems.ruling: ζητῶν is a participle with implied 1st person subject; χρῆσαι is 2nd singular imperative addressing reader, not 'use' as 1st person

The voice issue is real: the source uses the imperative χρῆσαι, not a first-person statement. The English should keep the imperative force, so 'I apply' has been changed to 'apply'.

edits.new: And the name of the second was Ruth. Ruth bears a type of the Gentiles, for she left behind her ancestral ways and was joined to the Israelite way of life. But we must ask how Ruth, being a Moabite, entered the assembly of God when the law forbids a Moabite from entering. And in seeking this, I apply the saying:

fixed: The English already says exactly what the source says for the opening formula, ancestral ways, and the rhetorical question. The only change needed is to make the speaker explicit in the final clause by changing 'apply' to 'I apply'.

last_rejected.quote: when the law forbids a Moabite from entering
last_rejected.source_quote: τοῦ νόμου ἀπαγορεύοντος μὴ εἰσελθεῖν Μοαβίτην εἰς Ἐκκλησίαν Θεοῦ
last_rejected.why: Greek has absolute prohibition (μὴ εἰσελθεῖν), not conditional 'when'; 'forbids...from entering' is ungrammatical English idiom.
last_rejected.fix: though the law forbids a Moabite to enter the assembly of God
last_rejected.ruling: 'when' renders temporal genitive participle ἀπαγορεύοντος; 'forbids from entering' is acceptable English for μὴ εἰσελθεῖν prohibition.
